title: Sierra Tech - Open Model & Tool Integration Discovery
summary: Initial discovery focused on Sierra Tech's selection between Redwood hosted, dedicated, and private options for running multi-language customer support models. Key constraints: mixed English/Spanish traffic, need for 64K+ context on long conversation threads, interest in function/tool calling for retrieval + actions, and strict data residency/KMS requirements. Redwood AE/SE explained model tradeoffs (open models / quantization / throughput), latency vs cost considerations, and proposed a short pilot and benchmarking run. Agreed next steps: security docs, pricing, and a technical deep-dive to run 5k/30k token latency tests on a candidate model.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-30
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moran (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Carlos Rivera (Sierra CTO), Maya Lin (Sierra ML Lead), Jordan Park (Product Manager)

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros from our side, I'm Alex, I own the account and will handle commercial. Priya's our solutions engineer, she will run through the tech bits.
[00:10] Carlos (Sierra CTO): Hey Alex, thanks. Carlos here, CTO. Maya and Jordan from my team.
[00:15] Maya (Sierra ML): Hi all.
[00:18] Jordan (Sierra PM): Morning.
[00:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Great. Goal for today is to understand your workload — traffic profiles, context needs, languages — and figure out whether Redwood hosted, dedicated, or private makes sense. We'll talk models and tool-calling too.

[01:05] Jordan: To give context, we run a customer support assistant that ingests tickets, call transcripts, and knowledge base docs. Primary is English but ~25% Spanish. We sometimes need to pull the entire ticket thread for context — threads can be long, like 10k-40k tokens.
[01:26] Maya: Also want to call internal tools — calendar, ticket updates — so function calling is important. Latency target for interactive support is under 800ms median on short prompts, but for long-thread synth we can tolerate higher.
[01:42] Priya: OK helpful. When you say 10k-40k tokens, is that the full context you need at inference time or can you prefix/summarize?
[01:50] Carlos: For escalation summaries we need most of it. For routine replies we can do prefixing but we'd like the option to feed full history for accurate summaries.

[02:20] Alex: Can you share current stack? Are you using any vector DB or retrieval?
[02:26] Maya: We're on AWS, vector DB is Pinecone for now. We have an internal ticket DB in RDS. Identity via Okta SAML. We need SOC 2 and customer audit trails.
[02:40] Priya: Good to know. On models: are you leaning open-source or commercial models? Any policy restrictions?
[02:47] Jordan: We prefer open models for cost and control but we need them to match the quality of hosted options. Latency and cost are big factors — we want sub-$0.02 per transaction if possible.

[03:10] Priya: High-level tradeoff: hosted Redwood API gives fastest time-to-value and built-in routing, but for predictable throughput and data isolation you might pick Dedicated. Private (VPC/on-prem) if strict data residency or no egress allowed. For models, open models like Mistral, LlamaX, and Meta variants can be quantized for cost but context length varies. Some open models now support 32k and 64k contexts (and a couple experimental 128k).

[03:55] Maya: What about tool-calling? We need structured outputs for function calls and safe execution.
[04:00] Priya: Redwood supports function/tool calling and structured outputs. We have examples of integrating RAG + function calls where retrieval provides chunks and the model emits JSON to drive actions. There are caveats when you use quantized weights — sometimes structured output fidelity drops; we'd run tests for that.

[04:35] Carlos: Can you talk about latency/throughput on 64k contexts?
[04:40] Priya: Sure — with long contexts the KV cache and attention kernels matter. On a Dedicated pool with A100/A800 class hardware, you can get reasonable throughput but per-token latency increases; typical response time for 20k token prompt plus 1k generation is in the 1.5–3s range depending on batch. For hosted, we automatically route to model variants optimized for cost.
[05:05] Jordan: That's OK for async summaries but for live chat we only feed recent 2-4k tokens.

[05:22] Maya: How do you handle multilingual quality? Spanish often has subtle tone issues.
[05:28] Priya: We do model recommendations by workload — some open models are trained multilingual and do well EN/ES. We also run evals using your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can run comparisons and suggest quantization profiles that retain EN/ES quality.

[06:00] Alex: Any customers doing a hybrid? Hosted for low-latency features and Dedicated for big-batch long-context jobs?
[06:07] Priya: Yes, common pattern is route conversational traffic to hosted variants for speed, and route long-form batch jobs to dedicated pools or private deployments for cost control. We can set routing policy per route.

[06:30] Carlos: Security — KMS and audit logs: we need customer-managed keys and per-request auditability.
[06:36] Priya: Redwood Private (VPC) supports customer KMS/HSM and full audit logs. Dedicated also supports KMS and more restricted data handling; hosted supports envelope encryption but for some customers we do bring-your-own-key options. We'll share SOC2 and architecture diagrams.

[07:02] Jordan: What about model drift and evals — we need to ensure quality doesn't regress after quantization or model swaps.
[07:08] Priya: We support continuous evals tied to your prompt sets and can alert on quality regressions. You can pin model versions and rollout via canary with auto-fallback. We'll show demo in the next deep dive.

[08:00] Maya: Pricing — what's the delta between hosted and dedicated?
[08:05] Alex: Hosted is usage-based per token; Dedicated is committed monthly capacity that reduces unit cost. For your volumes (estimated 1M interactions/month) Dedicated often becomes attractive after you hit steady throughput. We'll send a modeled cost comparison.

[08:35] Carlos: We want to try a candidate open model at 30k context and run tool-calling with retrieval — can Redwood run a benchmark?
[08:42] Priya: Yes. Suggested pilot: 1) Redwood runs benchmark on your sample prompts at 5k and 30k context lengths with model A (open candidate) under quantized and fp16 runs; 2) function-calling test with RAG + Pinecone integration; 3) measure latency and token cost.

[09:10] Jordan: Timeline? We're aiming to decide vendor in 3–4 weeks and have a pilot in April.
[09:16] Alex: That works. We can prioritize the benchmark and security pack.

[09:40] Maya: A few technical clarifications: how do you manage KV cache across requests when a user continues a thread?
[09:47] Priya: Redwood's runtime keeps per-session KV caches in memory on the serving nodes; you can pin sessions to nodes or use shared KV store depending on deployment. Note: when using Dedicated/GPU pools with autoscaling there are cache warmup considerations. We also support prefix caching for repeated context like policy text.

[10:10] Carlos: For private deployment, is there an offline on-prem installer?
[10:13] Priya: Yes, we have a Private on-prem package for air-gapped environments with offline install scripts. It integrates with customer KMS and local observability. We'll need your ops team's participation for networking and hardware validation.

[10:35] Jordan: Competitors — we evaluated an in-house Llama2 variant and also looked at managed Anthropic for red-teamed safety features. How do you compare on safety controls?
[10:44] Priya: We provide red-teaming tooling, prompt-level filters, and policy enforcement via the router; we can also integrate third-party safety stacks. For some regulated customers, Private deployment with local safety controls is preferred.

[11:20] Maya: A couple of gotchas we saw: quantization sometimes breaks structured JSON outputs; how do you mitigate?
[11:25] Priya: We test structured-output fidelity during Optimize runs. If a quantized model reduces fidelity, we either choose a different quant profile, use FP16 for tool-call endpoints, or use small-chain prompting patterns to improve consistency.

[12:00] Carlos: Ok, let's talk concrete next steps.
[12:05] Alex: I'll summarize — Redwood to: share security pack (SOC2, diagrams, KMS options), provide a cost model comparison (hosted vs dedicated vs private), run a two-part benchmark (5k and 30k context) with function-calling + Pinecone, and schedule a technical deep dive where Priya will walk through deployment choices.

[12:30] Jordan: Sounds good. Add timeline: benchmarks by Apr 6, security pack by Apr 2, deep dive week of Apr 6.

[12:40] Maya: Also please include a sample of eval results for Spanish prompts specifically.

[12:45] Priya: Will do — we'll include EN/ES evals and call fidelity tests.

[12:55] Alex: Any other questions?
[13:00] Carlos: None from me. Thanks.
[13:02] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[13:05] Alex: Great. We'll follow up with notes and the action items.

[13:20] End of recording.

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mishears: "Redwood Dedicate" for Dedicated, "K-V cash" for KV cache. Some speaker labels inferred.
